sentences.text: Antetonitrus ingenipes was a sauropodiform dinosaur that walked on four legs, marking a shift from the bipedal stance of its smaller ancestors.
Unlike later relatives that used their front limbs only for support, this animal used its forelimbs for grasping, aided by a twisted and flexible first finger.

The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — may have reached 8 to 10 meters in length, stood 1.5 to 2 meters at the hip, and weighed 5.6 metric tons, though unfused bones suggest it was not fully grown.
Its femur was slightly S-curved in lateral view, differing from the straight femur seen in other sauropods.
The first digit of the hand was twisted and flexible, capable of grasping, a unique adaptation for a dinosaur of its size.
The holotype specimen may have measured 8 to 10 meters in length, 1.5 to 2 meters in hip height, and 5.6 metric tons in body mass.

James Kitching discovered the fossils in 1981 in the Free State of South Africa, where they were initially labeled as Euskelosaurus before Adam Yates and James Kitching named Antetonitrus in a 2003 report.

The holotype consists of vertebrae and numerous bones from the forelimbs and hind limbs, presumed to be from one individual, while five additional limb bones from a smaller individual were also assigned to the genus.
The species name ingenipes means 'massive foot' because it shows early development of feet designed for weight support.
Antetonitrus was a quadrupedal herbivore that used its forelimbs for grasping rather than just for weight support.
The unfused neural arches suggest the holotype individual may not have been fully grown.
Antetonitrus belongs to the class Saurischia, the parent group of Antetonitrus is Lessemsauridae, and the animal belongs to the family Lessemsauridae.
Apaldetti et al. (2018) established the clade Lessemsauridae to include Antetonitrus, Lessemsaurus, and Ingentia.
Yates and Kitching classified Antetonitrus as a basal sauropod between more derived animals like Isanosaurus and more basal sauropods like Melanorosaurus.
Antetonitrus lived during the Early Jurassic period, specifically from the Hettangian to the Sinemurian stages, between 201.4 and 192.9 million years ago.
Studies indicate Antetonitrus was recovered from the Early Jurassic Upper Elliot Formation.

Antetonitrus is one of the oldest known sauropods chronologically, tied with others from the same formation, before Antetonitrus was recognized as a sauropod, Isanosaurus from Thailand was considered the oldest known sauropod.
Early sauropods and relatives were found worldwide because continents were united as Pangaea.
